title: HTTP/2 multiplexes. HTTP/1 lined up.
lede: HTTP/1.1 is one request at a time per connection (pipelining never really worked). Browsers open ~6 TCPs per host. HTTP/2 is many streams on one TLS connection: the JS, the CSS, the icons share the pipe. Head-of-line still exists at TCP (plate 285) — that is why HTTP/3 moved to QUIC.
diagram: Left: 6 connections, each a line of GETs. Right (hit): 1 connection, streams 1,3,5 in flight. Caption: a fat image still occupies bytes; multiplexing is not extra bandwidth. Server push mostly lost; you preload instead.
what: One TLS, many streams, binary frames. HPACK compresses headers. Priorities exist; implementations vary.
why: Why HTTP/2 made domain-sharding harmful (you split what should share). Plate 13 is the click; this is the reuse.
trap: Sharding assets across 8 hosts on HTTP/2. Assuming multiplexed means no blocking. HTTP/1.1 keepalive (plate 277) is not multiplexing.

title: HTTP/3 is QUIC on UDP.
lede: HTTP/3’s transport is QUIC, on UDP, with TLS 1.3 baked in (plate 279). Streams are independent: a lost packet stalls one stream, not the connection (unlike TCP+H2). 0-RTT can send app data on a returning visitor — with replay risk. Fall back to H2 is normal.
diagram: 1 UDP 443. 2 crypto + transport one handshake. 3 streams A,B; packet loss on A, B still moves. Caption: NAT (plate 284) and corporate firewalls still eat UDP; browsers retry H2.
what: HTTP semantics on a new transport. Connection migration (IP change) is a QUIC feature.
why: Mobile networks, lossy links. ‘Why is it UDP if UDP is unreliable?’ Reliability moved into QUIC.
trap: Blocking UDP/443 and blaming the app. 0-RTT for POST /pay (replay). Treating H3 as faster CPU — it can be more CPU.

title: Slow start is TCP feeling the pipe.
lede: A new TCP connection does not dump your 2MB JS at line rate. Congestion window (cwnd) starts small and doubles each RTT until loss or a threshold. Short flows live in slow start — that is why a new connection is expensive and reuse matters (plate 277).
diagram: Left: new TLS+TCP, cwnd tiny, many RTTs to fill. Right: warm connection, cwnd already open, bytes flow. Caption: BBR vs cubic are the controllers. You don’t set cwnd in app code; you avoid extra handshakes.
what: TCP probes the path. Loss shrinks the window. RTT is in the inner loop.
why: Latency budgets, CDNs near the user (plate 36), connection reuse, HTTP/2 (plate 274).
trap: Opening a connection per image. Measuring bandwidth with a 20KB payload still in slow start. ‘TCP is slow’ when you meant the handshake.

title: Keep-alive is reuse, not magic.
lede: Keep-alive (HTTP/1.1 default) leaves the TCP/TLS socket open for the next request. You skip handshake and slow start (plates 78, 276). Idle timeouts on LB, NAT, and origin will still kill it. A pool of idle sockets is the real design (plate 3).
diagram: Left: GET, FIN, GET — two TLS. Right: GET, GET on the same fd. Caption: Connection: close ends it. HTTP/2 is reuse plus multiplex. Proxies may coalesce or not (plate 286).
what: Reuse the session. Timeouts must agree (client, LB, server). Health: recycle idle connections.
why: APIs, browsers, gRPC channels. Tail latency is often a new handshake.
trap: Infinite idle. Mismatched timeouts: NAT 60s, you think 5min — mystery resets. One giant keep-alive and a greedy neighbor (H1).

title: DNS TTL is how long the lie lasts.
lede: DNS (plate 77) answers are cached for TTL seconds — by the OS, the browser, the resolver, sometimes longer. A 60s TTL is not a 60s cutover. Lower TTL before a failover; anycast can move without DNS. Clients you don’t control will be late.
diagram: 1 TTL 300. 2 you flip A record. 3 some resolvers still have the old for ≤300s, some longer (TTL clamping). Caption: NXDOMAIN is cached too (RFC 2308). Prefetch adds extra caches.
what: TTL is a permission to remember, not a guarantee to forget. Failover plans cannot assume instant DNS.
why: Blue/green, dual-region (plate 223), ‘we updated Route53 why are they still hitting us.’
trap: TTL 86400 and an emergency IP change. Using DNS as a load balancer for per-request fairness. Forgetting IPv6 AAAA still points at the corpse.

title: TLS 1.3 is one round trip.
lede: TLS 1.2: ~2 RTTs of crypto after TCP. TLS 1.3: 1-RTT handshake, keys from the first flight. 0-RTT on a session ticket can send data immediately — replayable, so not for POST /charge. Certificates still chain; clocks still matter (plate 78).
diagram: Left: TCP + 1.2, several round trips then GET. Right: 1.3, GET in the next RTT; 0-RTT GET on revisit. Caption: false start / session resumption are the 1.2 cousins. Always HTTPS; mixed content is the browser saying no.
what: Fewer RTTs, same PKI. 0-RTT is a cache of secrets with replay. ALPN picks h2/h3.
why: Tail latency on mobile RTTs of 100ms+. Why CDNs terminate TLS near the user.
trap: 0-RTT for non-idempotent POST (plate 29). Expired clocks on IoT. Assuming 1.3 means you can skip cert verification.

title: Secure, HttpOnly, Path. That's the cookie.
lede: The cookie is a response header: Set-Cookie: name=value; attributes. Secure = HTTPS only. HttpOnly = no JS (plate 232). Path and Domain scope where it is sent. SameSite (plate 233) is also an attribute. Missing flags are the vulnerability.
diagram: 1 Set-Cookie: sid=…; Secure; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=3600. 2 browser stores. 3 matching request includes Cookie: sid=…. Caption: Domain=.example.com sends to subdomains. Host-only (no Domain) is tighter. __Host- prefix requires Secure and Path=/.
what: Server-set credentials with a send policy. Size ~4KB. You cannot later add HttpOnly from JS.
why: Session design. Frontend plates 231–233 are the browser side; this is the header.
trap: Set-Cookie without Secure on an HTTPS site (still sent on a later HTTP navigation). Domain too wide. Multiple Set-Cookie overwritten because you used one header line wrong.

title: 304 is not a body.
lede: 304 Not Modified means ‘use what you cached.’ There is no payload. It is a successful revalidation after If-None-Match / If-Modified-Since (plate 245). CDNs emit 304 to the browser while they may have hit origin or their own store. Parsing 304 as JSON is undefined.
diagram: Left: 200 every time, full bytes. Right: 200 + ETag, then 304s. Caption: 304 is not 204. 204 No Content is a real empty success for an action. 304 is cache protocol.
what: Conditional GET. Validators live on the representation. 304 must not include a body per spec.
why: Repeat views, API clients with caches, CDNs. Bandwidth that is not in your origin graph.
trap: Client fetch().json() on 304. Origin that never sends ETag/Last-Modified so the CDN cannot 304. Using 304 for a POST.

title: gRPC is protobuf on HTTP/2.
lede: gRPC = HTTP/2 streams + protobuf payloads + a method path. Unary is one request/response. Server/client/bidi streams are extra frames on the same stream. Status is trailers (grpc-status), not only HTTP 200 — HTTP can be 200 with an application error. Browsers need gRPC-Web or a proxy.
diagram: Left: JSON REST, one HTTP code. Right: POST /pkg.Svc/Method, proto, trailers 0 OK / 14 UNAVAILABLE. Caption: deadlines are first-class. Load balancers must be h2-aware (plate 35). Protobuf is the schema; breaking fields is a contract (plate 83).
what: RPC on H2 with typed messages. Four streaming modes. Interceptors = middleware (plate 81).
why: Service meshes, mobile-to-backend, internal APIs. Interviews: how it maps to HTTP.
trap: JSON-over-gRPC cargo cult. Treating HTTP 200 as success. Browser talking native gRPC without a gateway. Changing proto field numbers.

title: UDP has no apology.
lede: TCP is a stream with retries, order, and congestion control. UDP is a datagram: send, maybe arrive, maybe twice, maybe never, maybe out of order. QUIC, DNS, video, games put reliability — if any — in the app. Use UDP when a late packet is worthless.
diagram: Left: TCP: loss → wait → retransmit → head-of-line (plate 285). Right: UDP: packet 4 drops, 5 still plays. Caption: ICMP unreachables and PMTU still exist. ‘UDP is faster’ is ‘UDP does less.’
what: No connection, no built-in retry. You own duplication and ordering. Firewalls treat it worse (plate 275).
why: Why games and H3 use UDP. Why you don’t put a bank transfer on raw UDP.
trap: Reimplementing TCP badly on UDP. Assuming order. Sending 64KB datagrams (fragmentation).

title: NAT is many insides, one outside.
lede: Network Address Translation: many private hosts share a public IP. The NAT box rewrites source IP:port and remembers a mapping. Inbound needs a mapping (hole punch, port forward, or a relay). Idle mappings expire — that is why keep-alives exist (plate 277) and why UDP NAT is fussy.
diagram: 1 10.0.0.5:54123 → NAT → 203.0.113.8:44123. 2 reply to 44123 maps back. 3 idle 60s, mapping gone, packets drop. Caption: CGNAT is NAT of NATs. Hairpin: two internals talking via the public IP.
what: A stateful rewrite. Outbound easy, inbound hard. STUN/TURN for WebRTC.
why: ‘It works on my laptop’ behind a home router. WebSockets and long-poll timeouts.
trap: Assuming the client’s IP is unique (logs, rate limits — plate 201). Server-initiated TCP to a phone. Trusting X-Forwarded-For without a hop policy.

title: One stall. The whole line waits.
lede: Head-of-line blocking: a lost packet at the front freezes everything behind it. HTTP/1: one request per connection, so HOL is the line of requests. HTTP/2: many streams, but TCP’s single ordered byte stream still HOL-blocks all streams on one loss. HTTP/3/QUIC: loss is per-stream (plate 275).
diagram: Left H1: req A huge, B waits on that connection. Right H2 over TCP: stream B’s frames sit behind a lost frame of A in the TCP seq. Caption: this is why H3 exists, not because UDP is fashionable.
what: HOL at HTTP vs HOL at TCP are different layers. Multiplex does not cancel TCP order.
why: Lossy wifi, one fat upload ruining the tab. Design: don’t pin unrelated calls on one fragile flow if you can help it — or move to H3.
trap: ‘H2 fixed HOL.’ One TCP to a sick peer and all streams freeze. Pipelining on H1 as if it were multiplex.

title: One connection can serve many hosts.
lede: HTTP/2 coalescing: if two hostnames share an IP and the cert covers both (SAN/wildcard), the browser may reuse one TLS connection. SNI said which name you wanted at handshake; after that, :authority on each stream picks the host. CDNs love this; origin isolation hates a surprise.
diagram: Left: a.cdn.com and b.cdn.com, same IP, cert DNS:*.cdn.com → one socket. Right: different IPs or certs → two. Caption: partition cookies by host still. Coalescing is a client optimization, not a server config you toggle by name.
what: Connection reuse across names when IP+cert allow. HTTP/1 cannot multiplex those names on one fd.
why: Why sharding on a CDN can collapse back to one connection (good). Why a wildcard cert has blast radius.
trap: Assuming Host: is isolated because you terminated TLS per domain on one IP — the client may still coalesce. Cookie Domain too wide (plate 280).
